newsitem.title: USA: Pixar can survive even if Jobs goes to Apple.
newsitem.headline: Pixar can survive even if Jobs goes to Apple.

text.p: When Pixar Animation Studios went public in 1995, investors flocked to grab a piece of the company because it had a hot new film called "Toy Story" and a sharp executive named Steve Jobs at the helm.
Now, as rumours of Jobs' pending return to Apple Computer Inc. gather momentum, some observers wonder what will happen to Pixar if Jobs is called to rescue the beleaguered computer maker.
Will Pixar, the studio that launched such characters as "Buzz Lightyear" and "Woody," continue to flourish without Jobs' undivided attention? Or will it stumble?
For now, most industry experts are betting the Point Richmond, Calif.-based studio will continue to turn out successful films, even if its charismatic leader is not there every day.

"I don't think Pixar is dependent on Steve Jobs to be very successful at creating animated feature films that have high commercial potential," said entertainment industry analyst Jeffrey Logsdon at Cruttendon Roth. "Steve's job is really not making the day-to-day production..."

Indeed, Jobs, who bought the computer division from LucasFilm in 1986 and transformed it into a highly successful animated film studio, is more of a dealmaker than a filmmaker. He recently signed a 10-year deal with Walt Disney Co. to provide Pixar with a stable distribution channel for its films and the marketing muscle to make sure they get into theatres.
He also made sure he held onto John Lasseter, the Academy-award winning director of "Toy Story," to keep Pixar humming along for years.
Last week, Pixar reported better-than-expected second quarter profits of $8.9 million, or 19 cents a share as revenues more than doubled to $14.4 million.
In the year-earlier period, Pixar earned $4.8 million, or 10 cents a share, on revenues of $6.9 million.
The results blew past analysts' average forecast of 9 cents a share and drove the stock price up $1.50 to $17.375 on Nasdaq last Friday. Pixar rose 36 cents to $16.375 on Wednesday.
Pixar, which creates computer-generated animated feature films, scored a big hit in October 1995 with its first film, "Toy Story," which took in $350 million worldwide at the box office.

Analysts say revenues during future quarters may trail off due to the lack of significant new products. But other projects, such as a planned direct-to-video sequel to "Toy Story," and the 1998 animated feature "A Bug's Life," should keep the market primed for the next burst of revenues.
Jobs, who became a billionaire when Pixar went public in November, is considered something of a visionary in Silicon Valley.

In 1976, Jobs and Stephen Wozniak set up shop in the garage of Jobs' parents home in Cupertino, Calif., to design a computer that would appeal to the masses. The result was the Apple II, a machine that helped usher in the era of personal computing.
In 1985, however, Jobs was ousted from the Cupertino, Calif.-based computer maker by then-Chief Executive Officer John Sculley.

Jobs, eager to remain a force in technology, went on to form a new company called Next Software Inc. and then Pixar. Earlier this year, Jobs sold Next to Apple for more than $400 million, setting the stage for his return to Apple as a special adviser to Chairman Gilbert Amelio.
When Amelio resigned under pressure earlier this month, many experts predicted Jobs would assume a more active role at Apple, but Jobs insisted he had no plans to return to Apple full time.
Last week, Jobs told industry analysts in a conference call that he was staying at Pixar.
However, reports continued to circulate in Silicon Valley that Jobs was prepared to accept the chairmanship of Apple while the company searches for a new chief executive.
Jobs was not available to comment on the reports and Apple officials declined to comment.
Some industry watchers believe Jobs could remain at Pixar even if he were to take the job at Apple.

"Steve Jobs is not a director and he's not making movies," said Keith Benjamin, an analyst at Robertson Stephens and Co. in San Francisco. "He's real important, but he doesn't need to be there 24 hours a day."
